title: Home Battery or WaterAccu: A deeper comparison
excerpt: Are you unsure about purchasing a home battery or WaterAccu? In this blog we offer you extra explanation about both systems.
contentHtml:
Twijfelt u over de aanschaf van een thuisbatterij of een WaterAccu? Of wilt u beter begrijpen hoe deze systemen werken? In dit blog bieden we u extra uitleg over beide systemen.

More storage of solar power desired

Returning power is becoming less and less advantageous. The netting scheme will be definitively abolished in the Netherlands in 2027. In addition, energy suppliers now charge costs for returning power, and while these feed-in costs are likely to be reduced in 2027, they will not disappear completely. This makes the return of electricity more financially unattractive.

This makes it increasingly important to use produced solar power itself as much as possible. There are a number of options for this, including the Solyx Energy WaterAccu. In this blog we compare the WaterAccu with another technology that contributes to the use of self-produced solar power, the home battery. Curious about the comparison between solar water heaters and the WaterAccu? Tjen read on here.

How does a home battery work?

  • Direct storage of electricity for later use (of electricity)
  • Different types with variations in technology
  • Costs 6,000 – 10,000 euros, including inverter and installation

The name says it all; a home battery is a rechargeable battery that is placed in households for more efficient use of power. The home battery is charged during the day via excess solar power, and if no solar power is available for other devices, the charged home battery can supply power. This saves power from the grid. The most common type is the lithium-ion battery, which can usually store the largest amount of power and last a long time.

Other types are the salt battery, the flow battery and the lead-acid battery. These batteries all use different processes and substances to store power. This means that some batteries are larger and heavier, and others last less. Thus, the lithium-ion battery is usually referred to when talking about a home battery. The storage capacity of home batteries differs on average between about 2.5-15 kWh.

How does the WaterAccu work?

  • Storage of electricity in warm water – you do not extract electricity from it, but warm water!
  • Capacity depending on boiler size
  • Costs 1,500-2,000 euros, including installation, electric boiler and Nymo

The WaterAccu is intended for heating tap water, which is used for showering and in the kitchen. The system consists of an electric boiler and a control device, the Nymo. The Nymo is connected to the smart meter and measures when power is supplied to the grid. With this information, the Nymo switches on the boiler’s power supply to heat tap water. The power is increased by exactly so much that no returned power is measured anymore.

In this way, only unused solar power is used to heat the tap water. In winter and on other days with little sunlight, the central heating combination can help to get the water up to temperature, or power from the grid can be used. The capacity of the WaterAccu depends on the volume of the boiler. A 100 liter boiler (suitable for a 2-person household) can store up to 7 kWh of power!

Comparison between the home battery and WaterAccu

The main difference between the home battery and the WaterAccu is the form of energy storage: a home battery stores energy to supply power, a WaterAccu stores energy to supply hot tap water. This makes the home battery more versatile since power can be used for different devices, while the WaterAccu is more specialized.

However, the versatility of the home battery is compromised by the costs: home batteries are usually very expensive. A standard home battery of 8 kWh can quickly cost 4,000 to 6,500 euros because of the raw materials needed to make one. There is also an inverter from 1,000 to 1,500 euros, and with installation included the total costs 6,000 to 10,000 euros. A WaterAccu costs on average between 1,500 – 2,000 euros, including installation.

What is best for me?

The cost of the home battery is the biggest reason for many people not to buy one yet. The WaterAccu is an easier product to purchase in this regard; although it uses the idle flow in a much more specialized way, most people need hot tap water daily. In addition, WaterAccu is easier to adjust to demand by simply changing the size of the boiler.

Moreover, one system does not necessarily exclude the other. The WaterAccu has a function to give priority to other devices that use idle solar power. In this way, the home battery can first be charged and then tap water can be heated. The following must be taken into account: if the home battery trades on the energy market (and returns to the grid), the WaterAccu will start unwanted. To combine this type of home battery and WaterAccu, an extra circuit is required. If the home battery is pure for using solar energy and does not return electricity to the grid, both systems work well side by side!
